chapters.title: Welcome — The World's First Public Museum
chapters.intro: Welcome to the museum that invented museums. Before you chase a single object, get the building itself into your head: a grand 1845 classical front hiding a light-filled 2009 museum stacked behind it. This first chapter orients you — facade, founder, and the route ahead.

subchapters.title: The Beaumont Street Facade
subchapters.text: Look at the front before you go in. Charles Cockerell's building of 1841 to 1845 is Greek Revival at full confidence: tall Ionic columns, a broad pediment, and stone the colour of Oxford honey. It was built for the university's art collections and the Taylor Institution next door, and the Ashmolean's older collections moved in during the 1890s under Keeper Arthur Evans. The modest street frontage lies — behind it, the 2009 redevelopment by Rick Mather Architects doubled the display space to five floors and around forty galleries. Free admission, half a million years inside. Take the free floor plan at the welcome desk; you will genuinely need it. The building is Grade I listed, and its portico faces the Randolph Hotel across the street — hotel and museum have been politely out-staring each other since the 1860s.
subchapters.directions: Enter through the main entrance on Beaumont Street and pause in the atrium.

subchapters.title: Elias Ashmole and 1683
subchapters.text: The museum takes its name from Elias Ashmole, the antiquarian and astrologer who gave his collection to Oxford University in 1677 on one condition: build a proper home for it. The university did, on Broad Street, and on 24 May 1683 the Ashmolean opened — often called the world's first public museum, and certainly Britain's first. That word public was the revolution. Before this, wonders lived in private houses, shown to friends. Here, anyone paying a small fee could walk in and look. The original Broad Street building still stands, now the History of Science Museum, and this Beaumont Street building is the collection's second, much larger home. Ashmole himself was a complicated benefactor — a royalist, astrologer and alchemist whose own collections of books, coins and curiosities joined the Tradescant material in the new museum.

subchapters.title: The Central Atrium and Cascading Staircase
subchapters.text: Stand in the atrium and look up. The 2009 rebuild cut a tall, daylit well through the building, with a cascading staircase zig-zagging between floors and bridges linking the old Cockerell wing to the new galleries. Orientation galleries on each floor — Exploring the Past, Ancient World, Asian Crossroads, West Meets East — state that floor's theme before you dive in. Practical tip: different parts of the same level are not always connected, a quirk of weaving old and new wings together. When a gallery seems to dead-end, return to the atrium lifts rather than hunting for a corridor that does not exist. The redevelopment cost around £61 million and added 39 new galleries; the museum closed for most of 2009 and reopened that November to considerable architectural applause.

subchapters.title: How This Guide Works
subchapters.text: Our route follows the museum's own logic, floor by floor. We start downstairs with the museum's biography and its themed galleries — money, writing, textiles — then walk the ground-floor ancient world from Egypt through Greece and Rome to the Cast Gallery. Upstairs we cross Asia, meet England's treasures and European art, and finish on the roof. You cannot see everything: nobody can, and the museum knows it, which is why its floor plan offers a '10 highlights in an hour' trail. Treat this guide as your highlights spine, then double back to whatever grabbed you. Everything is free except special exhibitions. The museum is busiest at weekend middays and quietest in the first and last hours of the day — plan your favourite gallery for those edges if you can.

chapters.caption: The Ashmolean on Beaumont Street — Charles Cockerell's neoclassical building, opened in 1845

chapters.title: The Ashmolean Story — Tradescants, a Dodo, and a Lantern
chapters.intro: Down on the lower ground floor, Gallery 2 tells the museum's own biography in objects. This is the essential first stop: nearly every famous oddity from the founding collection is here, and each one carries a story about how museums — and empires — collected the world.

subchapters.title: The Tradescants and the Ark
subchapters.text: The collection began with two gardeners. John Tradescant the Elder, gardener to kings and dukes, travelled and traded for rare plants and curious objects; his son, John the Younger, continued both the garden and the collecting. At their Lambeth house in London they kept a famous cabinet of curiosities nicknamed the Ark — stuffed animals, weapons, coins, costumes and wonders from every continent then known to Europeans. Visitors paid to marvel. When the younger Tradescant died, Elias Ashmole acquired the collection — in circumstances the Tradescant family disputed loudly — and it became the founding gift of this museum. Look for the surviving Ark objects displayed together here. The Ark's catalogue, published in 1656 as Musaeum Tradescantianum, was England's first museum catalogue — visitors could read the wonders before they travelled to Lambeth to see them.

subchapters.title: Powhatan's Mantle
subchapters.text: Look for the great hanging cloak of deerskin, decorated with thousands of tiny shell beads worked into figures of a man, animals and circles. This is Powhatan's Mantle, dating to the early 1600s, associated with Wahunsenacawh — Chief Powhatan, father of Pocahontas — paramount chief of the Algonquian peoples of Virginia when English settlers founded Jamestown in 1607. It reached the Tradescants through early colonial trade networks and is among the most important surviving Native American objects of its era. Stand back first for the beadwork figures, then step close: each bead was drilled, strung and sewn by hand. The label discusses its contested journey honestly — read it. The mantle is made of four deerskins and some 20,000 shell beads by some counts; its human figure may represent a chief, a deity, or the wearer himself.

subchapters.title: Guy Fawkes's Lantern
subchapters.text: In a case nearby sits an unremarkable-looking iron and horn lantern with an outsized biography: it is said to be the lantern Guy Fawkes was carrying when he was arrested beneath Parliament on 5 November 1605, guarding barrels of gunpowder intended to kill King James I. The lantern was given to the university in 1641 and has been a star object ever since — proof that a museum treasure need not be beautiful, only connected. Look at its shuttered design: a dark lantern, made to hide its own candle. Generations of Oxford visitors have stood exactly where you are standing, looking at exactly this object. The lantern's association was recorded when it was given by the family of Robert Heywood, a Westminster official involved in the plot's investigation — provenance rarely gets closer than that.

subchapters.title: The Oxford Dodo
subchapters.text: The Tradescant collection once held a complete stuffed dodo, the last seen in Europe. By 1755 it was so moth-eaten that curators destroyed it — saving only the head and one foot, which survive in Oxford's natural history collections today and are the world's only soft-tissue dodo remains. The Ashmolean Story tells this ruefully and well: it is a parable of early museums, which preserved wonders and lost them in equal measure. Lewis Carroll, an Oxford don, knew the dodo remains — one reason a self-caricaturing Dodo hands out prizes in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland. Ask at the desk whether dodo material is currently on display here or across the road. All that survives of the Oxford bird — head, foot and some feathers — is now the most scientifically valuable dodo material on Earth, sampled for DNA studies of the species.

subchapters.title: Lawrence of Arabia's Robes and Cromwell's Death Mask
subchapters.text: Two later arrivals show the collection still growing by fame. The white silk robes and dagger associated with T. E. Lawrence — Lawrence of Arabia — came to the museum after his First World War campaigns in the Middle East, gorgeous ceremonial dress that is also a document of Britain's imperial entanglement with the region. Nearby, look for a death mask of Oliver Cromwell, taken after the Lord Protector's death in 1658: the warts-and-all face of the man who ruled England as a republic. Together with coins, engravings and geological specimens from Ashmole's own collecting, these objects bridge the gap between cabinet of curiosities and modern museum. Lawrence's robes were presented by his family; he had worn such dress in the Arab Revolt and kept the garments as carefully as the museum keeps them now.

chapters.title: Exploring the Past — Writing, Textiles, and Conservation
chapters.intro: The rest of the lower ground floor is themed, not chronological: galleries on reading and writing, textiles, and the conservation studios. These quiet rooms are the museum's thinking made visible — how humans record, clothe and preserve — and most visitors walk straight past them. Don't.

subchapters.title: Reading and Writing — Gallery 6
subchapters.text: Gallery 6 follows humanity's most consequential invention across cultures. Look for Mesopotamian cuneiform tablets — wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay over four thousand years ago, among them material linked to the Kish Tablet tradition, some of the earliest writing anywhere. Then compare Egyptian hieroglyphs, Chinese characters and European manuscripts: every culture here solved the same problem, fixing speech so it could outlive the speaker, with completely different tools. Notice the materials as much as the scripts — clay, papyrus, bamboo, parchment, paper. Writing technology is physical first and intellectual second, and this small gallery makes that beautifully clear in about ten minutes. The gallery also holds Oxyrhynchus papyri — fragments of lost Greek literature and early Christian texts recovered from Egypt's rubbish mounds, a reminder that archives and waste paper are cousins.

subchapters.title: Textiles — Gallery 5
subchapters.text: Cloth rarely survives, which is why Gallery 5 matters: the Ashmolean's textile holdings, drawn from Eastern and Western collections alike, preserve what archaeology usually loses. Look for embroidered garments, woven hangings and fragments whose patterns travelled the Silk Roads faster than the people who made them — a motif woven in Persia reappearing in China or Italy is trade made visible. Textiles carried status, dowries and diplomacy; a ceremonial robe could be worth more than the building it was worn in. Read the labels for fibres and dyes: indigo, madder and insect reds were global commodities centuries before container ships. Fragile pieces rotate, so what you see is a snapshot of a vast store. Among the strengths here are embroideries and woven silks from China and the Islamic world, and the museum's celebrated collection of Palestinian and Arab dress, much of it collected a century ago.

subchapters.title: Conservation — Galleries 3 and 4
subchapters.text: Behind glass on this floor, the museum shows its homework: conservation studios where specialists clean paintings, stabilise textiles and piece together pottery, sometimes visible at work. Displays explain X-radiography, pigment analysis and the ethics of restoration — when to repair, when to leave damage as part of an object's biography. This is the Ashmolean's university identity on show: a research institution that happens to be open to everyone. If a conservator is working, watch for a few minutes. The patience is the point — a single ceramic join can take a day — and it reframes everything upstairs: nothing in this building looks after itself. The department's work feeds the museum's research publications; a single investigation — say, identifying a painting's pigments — can redirect how a whole gallery's labels are written.

subchapters.title: The Human Image
subchapters.text: On this floor the museum has also grouped displays around the human image — how cultures picture people, from ancient votive figures to portraiture. The theme is a useful lens for the whole visit: upstairs you will meet Cycladic figures that reduce a person to a folded-arm silhouette, Roman emperors whose wrinkles were political statements, and Renaissance portraits inventing individuality. Here, small objects from unrelated cultures sit side by side precisely so you compare solutions. A figure made to house a spirit, a figure made to flatter a patron and a figure made to remember the dead are doing different jobs in similar shapes. Keep that question — what is this image for? — in your pocket all day.

subchapters.title: The Vaulted Cafe and Shop Level
subchapters.text: This floor also holds the museum's vaulted cafe and its shop, and both are worth a deliberate pause rather than a guilty one. The cafe occupies the old basement vaults — brick arches, low light, a genuinely cosy contrast to the bright galleries — and is the sensible mid-visit reset before the ancient world. The shop is unusually well stocked with collection-based books and replicas; the souvenir guide and the highlights postcards are the useful buys. Lockers here take the large bags that cannot go into the galleries. Refuelled, head up to the ground floor: Egypt is waiting, and it rewards fresh eyes. The cafe's vaults are part of Cockerell's original 1840s basement — you are drinking coffee inside the building's foundations, among the oldest fabric in the museum.

chapters.title: The Money Gallery — The Biography of Coins
chapters.intro: Gallery 7, home of the Heberden Coin Room's displays, tells the whole biography of money in one room — from stamped lumps of electrum to paper and forgery. It is small, dense and quietly thrilling, and on Saturdays you may get to hold the real thing.

subchapters.title: The First Coins — Lydia and Electrum
subchapters.text: Start where money starts. In the seventh century BC, in Lydia in modern Turkey, someone stamped a lump of electrum — a natural gold-silver alloy from the river Pactolus — with a mark guaranteeing its weight. That stamp turned metal into coinage and changed commerce forever: value no longer needed weighing at every transaction. The Ashmolean's Heberden Coin Room is one of the world's great numismatic collections, and its earliest cases show these rough, bean-like first coins beside the polished money of later empires. Look closely at the lion-head stamps of the Lydian kings — the dynasty of Croesus, whose name still means rich. Within a generation, Lydia's innovation spread to the Greek cities of Ionia; within two centuries, coinage had reached from Spain to India — history's fastest financial technology transfer.

subchapters.title: Athens' Owl — Money as Civic Advertising
subchapters.text: Greek city-states turned coins into tiny billboards. Find the silver tetradrachms of Athens: Athena's head on one side, her owl on the other, struck from silver mined at Laurion. For two centuries this was the trusted trade coin of the Mediterranean — the dollar of its day — and its design barely changed, because recognisability was the brand. Other cities advertised their own symbols: a turtle for Aegina, a horse for Corinth. In a world without newspapers, the coin in every purse was mass media. The gallery's Greek cases are arranged city by city, so you can watch rival states compete in miniature, in silver. So trusted was the owl that imitations were struck as far away as Egypt and Arabia — ancient counterfeits and compliments at once, several of which sit in these same cases.

subchapters.title: Roman Coins — Propaganda You Could Spend
subchapters.text: Rome industrialised the message. An emperor's portrait and titles went onto coins that reached every corner of the empire, announcing accessions, victories and building projects to people who would never see Rome. Look for the portrait sequence — you can watch emperors age, and regimes change, in a single case. The displays also show money failing: debased coins with shrinking silver content chart third-century inflation more honestly than any text. And find the forgeries, ancient and modern. Wherever money is trusted, someone counterfeits it; the Heberden displays treat fakers as part of the story, not an embarrassment. The Heberden Coin Room's total holdings run to well over 300,000 coins and medals, one of the largest numismatic collections in the world, of which this gallery shows a fraction.

subchapters.title: Money Beyond Coins
subchapters.text: Not all money clinks. This gallery ranges across cowrie shells traded from Africa to Asia, metal bars, tally sticks and early paper money from China, which was printing currency centuries before Europe dared. The point lands gently: money is trust made physical, and the physical form can be almost anything a community agrees to honour. Look for the displays on hoards — buried pots of coins that are time capsules of fear, hidden in invasions and never recovered — and on the Oxford Crown, a famous Civil War-era coin struck in this city in 1644 when Charles I held his wartime court here. Oxford money, made in a siege, in an Oxford museum: full circle. Chinese paper money of the Ming dynasty displayed here is among the earliest surviving anywhere — large, mulberry-bark notes printed with stern warnings to counterfeiters, punishable by death.

subchapters.title: Holding History — Coin Handling
subchapters.text: If your visit falls on a Saturday, check the gallery for the hands-on coin-handling sessions, when volunteers place real historic coins in visitors' palms. There is something quietly thrilling about a two-thousand-year-old coin still doing its original job — being held, weighed, wondered at. Even on other days, the gallery's magnifiers and touchable replicas reward slowing down. Before you leave, find one coin from a place you have been and one from a civilisation you cannot pronounce. Money connects both. Then head upstairs to the ground floor, where the ancient world galleries begin with Egypt at its origins. The Coin Room also runs identification days, when visitors bring in found coins — detectorists' finds from Oxfordshire fields regularly turn out to be Roman, Saxon or Civil War issues.
subchapters.directions: From the Money Gallery, take the atrium lift or stairs up to the Ground Floor for Egypt, Galleries 22–27.

chapters.caption: The Money Gallery — coins from the first Lydian issues to the modern world

chapters.title: Ancient Egypt at Its Origins — Before the Pharaohs
chapters.intro: Galleries 22 to 27 hold one of Europe's great Egyptian collections, and its particular glory is the beginning: pre-Dynastic Egypt, the thousands of years before the pharaohs, where the Ashmolean's holdings are the most significant outside Cairo. Slow down — these rooms reward it more than any others in the museum.

subchapters.title: Pre-Dynastic Egypt — Gallery 22
subchapters.text: Begin with a world still inventing itself. Before pyramids, before hieroglyphic king lists, farming communities along the Nile were producing pottery painted with boats, dancers and desert animals, and carving slate palettes for grinding eye paint. The Ashmolean's pre-Dynastic collection — much of it from the pioneering excavations of Flinders Petrie, who more or less invented scientific archaeology in Egypt — is the finest of its kind outside Cairo. Look for the beaded dresses, reconstructed bead by bead, and the hippopotamus figurines in blue faience. Petrie's genius was sequence dating: sorting pottery styles to build a chronology for an age without written records. These quiet cases are that revolution's evidence. Petrie's Egyptian work was funded partly by public subscription through the Egypt Exploration Fund; ordinary Victorian subscribers received shares of the finds, which is one route by which objects reached Oxford.

subchapters.title: The Narmer and Scorpion Maceheads
subchapters.text: Look for two carved stone maceheads that bookend Egypt's birth as a state. The Scorpion Macehead, from Hierakonpolis, shows a king — named for the scorpion beside his head — performing a ceremonial act around 3100 BC, one of the earliest images of Egyptian kingship. The Narmer Macehead celebrates Narmer, the king credited with unifying Upper and Lower Egypt. These are not weapons but votive offerings, oversized and ceremonial, deposited in a temple. Together with the famous Narmer Palette in Cairo, they are primary documents of the moment Egypt became Egypt — history's first nation-state announcing itself in carved limestone, found by Oxford-linked excavations. Both maceheads were excavated in the Main Deposit at Hierakonpolis in 1897 to 1898, a single temple pit that yielded a founding archive of Egypt's first kings.

subchapters.title: Dynastic Egypt and Sudan — Gallery 23
subchapters.text: The story continues into the age of the pharaohs, and widens south into Sudan and Nubia — a reminder that Egyptian civilisation was African and riverine, not a Mediterranean sideshow. Look for sculpture, stelae inscribed with prayers and biographies, and material from Nubian cultures that traded with, fought and sometimes ruled Egypt: in the eighth century BC, Kushite kings from Sudan conquered Egypt and reigned as its Twenty-Fifth Dynasty. The gallery's masterpiece from that era is coming in the next chapter's neighbour case — the Shrine of Taharqa — but here, notice the jewellery and amulets: small, personal magic, worn for protection in life and death alike. Oxford's Griffith Institute, the university's Egyptology centre, holds Howard Carter's complete excavation archive for Tutankhamun's tomb — the research depth behind these galleries is a staircase away.

subchapters.title: The Shrine of Taharqa
subchapters.text: Find the sandstone shrine of King Taharqa, the Kushite pharaoh who ruled Egypt around 690 to 664 BC. It comes from Kawa in Sudan, was excavated by Oxford teams in the 1930s, and is one of the largest Sudanese objects in Britain — a complete small temple shrine, its walls carved with the king before the gods. Taharqa is a giant figure of the ancient world: he appears in the Bible as Tirhakah, and his pyramid at Nuri still stands in Sudan. Notice how the carving blends Egyptian iconography with Kushite features. This single object justifies the gallery's joint title: Egypt and Sudan, one river, intertwined histories. Taharqa also built at Karnak and is named in the Second Book of Kings; his shrine's journey from Kawa to Oxford in the 1930s involved Nile barges and considerable diplomacy.

subchapters.title: Everyday Life Along the Nile
subchapters.text: Between the monuments, look for the life: wooden models of bakers, brewers and boat crews made to serve their owners eternally; cosmetics pots and mirrors; board games, including senet, the race game Egyptians played for three thousand years and buried with kings. The Egyptians were practical about eternity — the afterlife needed staff, food and entertainment, so they supplied them in model form. Also watch for the museum's candid labels about how this material reached Oxford: excavation shares divided under British administration in Egypt and Sudan. The museum does not hide that colonial context, and reading those labels is part of a modern visit. Look also for the wooden toilet seat and the linen sheets in the domestic cases — Egyptian daily life survives here in objects too humble for tomb-robbers to steal.

chapters.caption: Life after death in ancient Egypt — among the finest pre-Dynastic collections outside Cairo

chapters.title: Life After Death — Mummies, Amarna, and Eternity
chapters.intro: The Egypt galleries climax with death — which for Egyptians was less an ending than a change of address. Coffins, mummies and grave goods fill these rooms, alongside the revolutionary art of Akhenaten's Amarna period, when Egypt briefly worshipped one god and reinvented its image of the human body.

subchapters.title: Life After Death — Gallery 24
subchapters.text: Gallery 24 is devoted to the Egyptian afterlife, and its centrepiece tradition is mummification: the seventy-day process of drying, anointing and wrapping a body so the soul would recognise its home. Look for the mummy of Meresamun and the painted coffins whose spells and images — from the Book of the Dead — equipped the deceased to navigate the underworld's trials, including the weighing of the heart against a feather. Canopic jars held the removed organs, each guarded by a son of Horus. Everything here is equipment: eternity, for Egyptians, was a logistics problem, and they solved it beautifully. Meresamun was a temple singer of Amun at Thebes around 800 BC; her mummy and coffins were excavated at Deir el-Medina's wider necropolis region and reached Oxford in the 19th century.

subchapters.title: Painted Coffins and Grave Goods
subchapters.text: Slow down at the coffin cases. The nested wooden coffins are painted inside and out with gods, goddesses and protective texts — the decoration is the function, armour for the journey west. Shabti figures, the little servant statuettes buried in their hundreds, were inscribed with a spell obliging them to answer when the deceased was called to labour in the fields of the afterlife: even in paradise, Egyptians expected paperwork. Look, too, for heart scarabs placed over the chest, pleading with the heart not to betray its owner at the weighing. The craftsmanship is intimate — these objects were made by people preparing, carefully, for forever. Some coffins here were reused — ancient Egyptians, thrifty as anyone, repainted earlier coffins for new owners, and X-rays and inscriptions under the paint sometimes reveal the first occupant.

subchapters.title: The Amarna Revolution — Gallery 25
subchapters.text: In the fourteenth century BC, Pharaoh Akhenaten did something unthinkable: he demoted Egypt's many gods, elevated the sun disc, the Aten, moved the capital to a new city, Amarna, and let art change with theology. Bodies elongate, bellies swell, faces soften into androgyny — the Amarna style is instantly recognisable and still startling. Gallery 25 gathers sculpture and fragments from that experiment, including material linked to Akhenaten's queen Nefertiti and to the young Tutankhamun, who inherited and then reversed the revolution. Stand before the royal images and consider the speed of it: within one reign, a thousand-year visual tradition was deliberately broken. Amarna was excavated by Petrie in 1891 to 1892 and later by the Egypt Exploration Society; the Ashmolean's share includes plaster portrait studies from the royal workshops.

subchapters.title: Egypt in the Roman World — Gallery 26 and Beyond
subchapters.text: The final Egypt rooms follow the civilisation into its long afterlife under Greek and Roman rule — Ptolemaic temples, Roman-era mummy portraits of startling realism painted on wood panels, and the slow merging of Egyptian religion with the classical world. Those portraits deserve your closest look: encaustic faces, individual and alive, staring out across two thousand years. Egypt's story in this museum does not end with Cleopatra; it dissolves into the Mediterranean world you are about to enter on this same floor. When you are ready, the Aegean galleries are next — Crete, and the oldest civilisations of Europe. The Faiyum mummy portraits, painted in encaustic wax on limewood, were attached over the faces of the mummified dead — portrait and coffin in one, startlingly lifelike at eighteen centuries' distance.

chapters.title: The Aegean World — Minoans, Mycenae, and Arthur Evans
chapters.intro: Gallery 20 holds the Ashmolean's Aegean collections, among the most important outside Greece — much of it from Sir Arthur Evans, the museum's own Keeper, who uncovered the palace at Knossos and named the Minoans. Here Europe's story begins, in clay, bronze and startlingly modern-looking marble.

subchapters.title: Sir Arthur Evans and Knossos
subchapters.text: Arthur Evans became Keeper of the Ashmolean in 1884 and transformed it — but his fame rests on Crete. From 1900 he excavated at Knossos, revealing a vast Bronze Age palace of storerooms, frescoes and plumbing, and named its civilisation Minoan, after the legendary King Minos of the labyrinth and the Minotaur. Evans rebuilt parts of Knossos in reinforced concrete, controversially, and his interpretations — a peaceful, elegant, almost modern civilisation — still shape how we picture the Minoans. The Ashmolean, as his museum, holds excavation material, archives and objects no other British museum can match. You are looking at the spoils of one man's magnificent obsession. Evans bought the Knossos site outright with his own fortune — he was heir to a paper-manufacturing business — and employed over a hundred workmen in the first season alone.

subchapters.title: The Octopus Jar
subchapters.text: Look for the large stirrup jar painted with a gloriously sprawling octopus, made at Knossos around 1450 to 1400 BC. The octopus's tentacles wrap the vessel's curves so the animal seems to swim around it — the so-called Marine Style, the high point of Minoan pottery painting. It is one of the museum's ten official highlights, and rightly: three and a half thousand years old, and the design feels like it was drawn yesterday. Beside it, look for the great storage pithoi from the palace magazines — jars taller than a person, which held the oil, wine and grain that were Knossos's real wealth. The jar was a stirrup jar, made for storing and pouring precious oil; its narrow neck and false spout were engineering for liquids worth more than wine.

subchapters.title: Cycladic Figures
subchapters.text: In a quieter case, look for white marble figures from the Cyclades islands, carved around 2800 BC and earlier: folded arms, tilted faces, bodies reduced to a few serene planes. They look like works by a modern sculptor — and modern sculptors noticed: the Cycladic style influenced artists from Brâncuși to Barbara Hepworth. Most were grave goods; traces of pigment show they were once painted, eyes and hair picked out in colour. Their original purpose remains debated — goddesses, ancestors, companions for the dead — and that mystery is part of their pull. Stand a moment: these are among the oldest artworks in the building, and among the most contemporary-looking. Most Cycladic figures come from graves on islands such as Keros and Naxos; their marble was quarried locally and shaped with obsidian and emery tools, then polished with pumice.

subchapters.title: Mycenae and the Road to Greece
subchapters.text: The Aegean story darkens into the Mycenaean world — the fortified, gold-rich citadels of mainland Greece, the culture behind Homer's tales of Troy. Look for Linear B tablets' world in objects: weapons, gold work and pottery from the centuries around 1200 BC, when the Bronze Age palace systems collapsed in fire and upheaval. Evans believed the Minoans were peace-loving; the Mycenaeans left no such illusion. This gallery is the hinge of the ground floor: behind you, Egypt and the Near East; ahead, classical Greece, which inherited the Aegean's scripts, gods and sea-routes and turned them into something new. Linear B, the Mycenaean script displayed in this story, was deciphered in 1952 by Michael Ventris — proving the palace bureaucrats of 1200 BC were writing an early form of Greek.

chapters.title: The Greek World and Its Sculpture
chapters.intro: Galleries 16 and 21 take you from Greek city-states to the great sculpture collection, anchored by the Arundel Marbles. Greece here is not a marble cliché but a competitive, trading, arguing civilisation — and its inscriptions, kept in unusual strength, let it speak in its own words.

subchapters.title: The Greek World — Gallery 16
subchapters.text: Gallery 16 maps a civilisation spread by sea: city-states from Spain to Syria, connected by trade, colonies and a shared language. The Ashmolean is especially strong in Athenian pottery — look for black-figure and red-figure vases whose painted scenes are our best picture book of Greek myth, athletics, drinking parties and daily life. A vase painter signed some of these; craftsmen were celebrities. Also find the material of Alexander the Great's era, when Greek culture stretched to Egypt and Afghanistan. The gallery's quiet thesis: Greekness was portable. Wherever the pottery, coins and gods travelled, Greece happened there. The museum's Greek vase collection is one of Britain's finest for study, with the teaching collection used by Oxford's classics students, who still handle ancient pottery in supervised sessions.

subchapters.title: Greek and Roman Sculpture — Gallery 21
subchapters.text: The sculpture gallery is where you meet antiquity face to face. Portrait busts preserve real individuals — emperors with every wrinkle of power intact, private citizens with haircuts datable to a decade. Greek originals stand beside Roman copies of Greek masterpieces, which is how most classical sculpture survives: Rome mass-produced Greek genius for villa gardens across an empire. Get close. Marble this worked repays inches, not metres — the drill-work in hair, the undercut eyelids. The gallery is intimate by design, closer to a picture cabinet than a warehouse hall, and you can stand nose to nose with a Roman emperor. He won't mind; he's had two thousand years of it. Many pieces here arrived via the great 17th and 18th-century collections — Arundel, Pomfret and others — making this gallery a history of English collecting as much as of classical art.

subchapters.title: The Arundel Marbles
subchapters.text: Among the sculpture, honour the Arundel Marbles: classical antiquities collected in the early 1600s by Thomas Howard, Earl of Arundel, one of England's first great collectors, whose agents scoured the Ottoman Greek world for statues and inscriptions. Donated to Oxford in the 1660s, they are among the founding antiquities of this museum — older than the museum itself. Their arrival made Oxford a centre for classical study a generation before the Ashmolean opened. Look for the weathered inscribed stones among the figures: to seventeenth-century scholars, the texts mattered as much as the statues, and some are still cited by historians today. Arundel's collection was partly scattered after his death in the Civil War era; Oxford's portion arrived through his grandson's gift, and the rescued inscriptions are still called the Oxford Marbles.

subchapters.title: The Parian Marble and the Metrological Relief
subchapters.text: Two inscribed stones deserve a hunt. The Parian Marble, carved on Paros around 264 BC, is the earliest surviving Greek chronological table — a timeline of myth and history from the legendary King Cecrops down to its own day, our earliest example of a civilisation writing its own timeline. The Metrological Relief, from around 450 BC, shows a man's outstretched arms and carved measures — the fathom, foot and fist — a standard-measures board in marble, part sculpture, part bureau of standards. Together they show what this collection does best: objects that are simultaneously art and data. The Parian Marble's chronicle begins in myth — it dates Cecrops, Athens' legendary first king, to 1581 BC — and continues into sober history, a single stone straddling both kinds of past.

subchapters.title: Greek Inscriptions
subchapters.text: Oxford's Greek inscription collection is a research treasure hiding in plain sight — hundreds of carved texts: decrees, dedications, epitaphs, casualty lists. An epitaph gives you a named individual, a family, a grief, in a dozen words; a casualty list gives you a war's cost, name by name. Translations accompany the major pieces, so read a few aloud, quietly. This is the ancient world unmediated — not a historian's summary but the stone itself, cut by a mason who charged by the letter. If the Aegean galleries showed Greece being born, these stones show Greeks talking. It is the most human sound in the museum, and it is silent. The collection includes fragments of the Athenian tribute lists, recording payments from Athens' allies — imperial accounting in marble, and key evidence for how the Athenian empire was financed.

chapters.caption: Greek and Roman sculpture — the Arundel Marbles and 2,500 years of Mediterranean art

chapters.title: Rome, Its Neighbours, and the Ancient Near East
chapters.intro: The ground floor's remaining ancient galleries fill in the map: Italy before Rome, Rome itself, Cyprus the crossroads island, European prehistory, and the Ancient Middle East of the first cities and first writing. Together they stop the classical world looking like a two-country story.

subchapters.title: Italy Before Rome — Gallery 15
subchapters.text: Rome had neighbours, rivals and teachers. Gallery 15 covers Italy from 800 to 400 BC: Etruscans, whose bronze work, tomb goods and enigmatic language fascinated and fed Rome; Italic peoples with their own armour, jewellery and votive offerings. Look for Etruscan bronzes — mirrors engraved with mythological scenes, used by women whose status in Etruscan society startled Greek and Roman commentators. The point of the room is humility for the next one: when Rome arrives, it arrives as an inheritor and imitator, borrowing Etruscan kingship symbols, Greek gods and everyone else's engineering. Empires rarely invent; they absorb. Etruscan bucchero pottery — black, burnished and metallic-looking — fills several cases here; it imitated bronze tableware for those who wanted the look at a clay price.

subchapters.title: Rome — Gallery 13
subchapters.text: Gallery 13 follows Rome from republic to empire, roughly 400 BC to AD 300, through the material of daily life as much as monuments: red-gloss tableware mass-produced and traded empire-wide, glass, lamps, brooches, tools. A Roman provincial's dinner set looked much the same from Britain to Syria — antiquity's first consumer standardisation. Look for the portrait heads' sterner cousins here, and for objects from Roman Britain that close the loop with home. The gallery pairs naturally with the sculpture you have just seen: there, Rome's image; here, Rome's stuff. Empires run on stuff — supply chains, standard measures, replaceable parts — and this room proves it in pottery. Look for the lead curse tablets and inscribed altars among the everyday objects: provincial Romans cursed thieves, rivals and faithless lovers in writing, and folded the evidence into springs and graves.

subchapters.title: Ancient Cyprus — Gallery 18
subchapters.text: Cyprus sat at the Mediterranean's crossroads, and Gallery 18 shows an island civilisation absorbing Egypt, the Near East and Greece while staying stubbornly itself. Copper made Cyprus rich — the island's name may derive from the metal — and its pottery, terracotta figures and sculpture blend influences with cheerful confidence. Look for the limestone votive statues, rows of worshippers offered to sanctuaries, their costumes a fashion archive of the ancient eastern Mediterranean. Cyprus is the ground floor's argument in miniature: cultures here were never sealed boxes. Everything traded, everything borrowed, and the borrowing is the story the whole floor tells. The museum's Cyprus collection owes much to 19th-century excavations and to the island's position under British administration from 1878, when antiquities flowed to British museums in quantity.

subchapters.title: Ancient Middle East — Gallery 19
subchapters.text: Gallery 19 reaches back to the first cities: Mesopotamia, modern Iraq, where writing, law and the wheel appear. Look for cylinder seals — tiny carved stone rollers whose rolled impression signed documents and marked property, each one a miniature artwork in reverse — and cuneiform tablets recording sales, school exercises and omens. The Kish material connects to the earliest writing in the Reading and Writing gallery downstairs. Stand here a second and recalibrate the visit: Greece and Egypt, for all their glory, were latecomers. The administrative, mathematical world they inherited was invented here, in mud-brick cities, by people whose names we mostly know from their receipts. The famous Kish Tablet tradition represented here dates to around 3500 BC — picture-signs for commodities, from a city in modern Iraq, older than the pyramids by a millennium.

subchapters.title: European Prehistory — Gallery 17
subchapters.text: Finally, home ground: Gallery 17 covers prehistoric Europe, including Britain before Rome — flint tools, Bronze Age metalwork and the long, unwritten millennia in which the Ashmolean's own half-million-year claim begins. Look for the Abingdon Sword, a superb late Anglo-Saxon blade found just south of Oxford, its hilt inlaid with silver — the England galleries' story starting early, in a river town you could cycle to this afternoon. Prehistory galleries can feel austere, but the timescales reframe everything: the pyramids are closer in time to us than to some of the tools in these cases. You have now walked the whole ancient ground floor. The Abingdon Sword was found in the Thames at Abingdon in 1874; its pattern-welded blade and silver-inlaid hilt mark it as a weapon of the highest status in late Saxon England.

chapters.title: The Cast Gallery — A Garden of Plaster Gods
chapters.intro: Gallery 14 is the museum's most atmospheric room: over a thousand plaster casts of Greek and Roman masterpieces, glowing white in one of Cockerell's original nineteenth-century spaces. In the age before cheap travel, this was how Oxford studied the classical world. Time has made the copies precious in their own right.

subchapters.title: Why Casts? Studying Antiquity Without Travel
subchapters.text: These are exact plaster copies of famous sculptures scattered across Europe's museums, assembled from the 1700s onward so students could study classical art without leaving Beaumont Street. In the age before photography, cast collections were serious scholarly infrastructure; almost every great university had one, and almost all were later thrown out as unfashionable. The Ashmolean kept its — over 1,000 casts — one of the most complete survivals in Britain. Walk the rows slowly: this is a greatest-hits album of classical sculpture, the canon as the Victorians understood it, gathered into a single room of luminous white figures. The Ashmolean's cast collection, founded in its modern form in the 1880s, now numbers over 1,000 pieces and is one of the largest and best-preserved in Britain.

subchapters.title: The Kritios Boy
subchapters.text: Look for the Kritios Boy, the calm, revolutionary figure from about 480 BC, cast from the original found on the Athenian Acropolis. He matters out of all proportion to his size: he is among the first Greek statues to stand with weight shifted onto one leg — contrapposto — the moment Greek sculpture learned to relax, and with it, to look alive. Compare him with the stiff, frontal figures around him and the breakthrough is obvious: a body thinking, not posing. The original marble was buried after the Persian sack of Athens; this plaster ambassador has been teaching Oxford students that turning point for over a century. The original Kritios Boy was found in the Perserschutt — the rubble Athens buried after the Persians sacked the Acropolis in 480 BC — which is why this calm face survives at all.

subchapters.title: Casts That Outlast Their Originals
subchapters.text: Here is the room's unexpected twist: many casts were moulded from originals that have since been damaged — by acid rain, pollution, war and well-meaning cleaning. In places, the Oxford plaster preserves surface details the marble in Athens or Rome has lost, so the copy is now the better document, and scholars travel to study the casts. It inverts the usual hierarchy of original over reproduction, and the gallery's labels make the point proudly. Look at hands, drapery edges and inscriptions where the label notes a cast's unique evidence. A copy made for teaching became, by surviving, an archive. Casts here include pieces from the Parthenon sculptures and the Bassae frieze whose originals have lost surface to pollution and handling since the Oxford moulds were taken.

subchapters.title: The Room Itself
subchapters.text: Finally, enjoy the architecture: this is one of the original 19th-century galleries of Cockerell's building, deliberately left atmospheric in the 2009 rebuild — tall, top-lit, and hushed in a way the new galleries are not. On a quiet morning it feels like a garden of sleeping gods, and photographers love the raking light across white plaster. The Cast Gallery is also a working study collection: art history and classical archaeology students still draw and measure here. From this Victorian survivor, we climb — literally — to Asia, where the museum's second great theme, cultures crossing, takes over the upper floors. The gallery was designed by Cockerell as part of the 1840s building and is among the few interiors to survive the 2009 redevelopment essentially as the Victorians knew it.
subchapters.directions: From the Cast Gallery, return to the atrium and ride up to Level 1 for Asian Crossroads.

chapters.caption: The Cast Gallery — plaster casts of Greek and Roman masterpieces, some finer than the weathered originals

chapters.title: Asian Crossroads — China, India, and the Silk Roads
chapters.intro: Levels 1 and 2 retell Asia as the museum's organising idea: crossroads. Cultures traded goods, religions and designs along the Silk Roads for two thousand years. We start on Level 1 with early China and India, then rise to the Islamic world and Mughal splendour.

subchapters.title: China to AD 800 — Gallery 10
subchapters.text: Start with China's long beginning: Neolithic painted pottery, bronze ritual vessels whose taotie masks still glare after three thousand years, and the tomb figures of the Tang dynasty — including the camel, laden and bellowing, that is one of the museum's official highlights. Tang tomb figures, mingqi, were buried to serve the dead: officials, musicians, horses and camels from the Silk Road caravans. The camel is the gallery's thesis in clay — China's wealth walked west on camels and returned as glass, silver and ideas. Look for the green-glazed and three-colour sancai wares; their palette is unmistakably Tang. The Tang camel, a museum highlight, was excavated from a tomb near Xi'an; such mingqi were mass-produced from moulds, then hand-painted — an industry serving the dead.

subchapters.title: Chinese Paintings — Gallery 11
subchapters.text: Next door, lower your voice and your pace: the Chinese paintings gallery shows scrolls and album leaves in rotation, because works on silk and paper fade. The Ashmolean's collection of modern Chinese painting is among Europe's finest, and its earlier holdings include landscapes in which a whole mountain world unrolls in a few brushstrokes, empty space doing half the work. Handscrolls were unrolled section by section, an arm's length at a time — painting as slow cinema. If a scroll is fully displayed, walk its length and watch the journey accumulate: a bridge, a boat, a scholar's hut, weather arriving. The gallery's holdings include works given by the painter Guo Daosen and the great collection formed by Jose Mauricio Reyes, making Oxford a serious address for modern Chinese art.

subchapters.title: India to AD 600 — Gallery 12
subchapters.text: Gallery 12 gives early India its own weight: sculpture from the centuries when Buddhism, Hinduism and Jainism were all taking visual form. Look for the great early Buddha images — the museum's highlight Buddha of about AD 200 comes from the world this gallery builds — shown with the serene, downward gaze and hand gestures, mudras, that encode teaching, meditation and fearlessness. Gandharan sculpture, from the northwest, shows Greek influence carried east by Alexander's successors: a Buddha with Apollo's hair and a Roman's drapery. No gallery in the building demonstrates 'crossroads' better. The ideas travelled; so did the faces. The early Buddha images here come largely from Mathura and Gandhara, the twin workshops of the Kushan empire — one Indian in style, one Greco-Roman, both producing icons for the same faith.

subchapters.title: Asian Crossroads Orientation — Gallery 28
subchapters.text: Level 1's orientation gallery, Gallery 28, states the floor's argument with objects chosen as ambassadors: a textile here, a coin there, a vessel that is Chinese in shape and Islamic in decoration. Spend three minutes here rather than skipping it — it teaches you to spot hybrids, and the upper floors are full of them. The Silk Roads were not a single road but a relay network across steppe, desert and sea, and nothing that travelled the whole way arrived unchanged. Buddhism itself is the supreme example: an Indian religion that reached Japan transformed, carrying Greek faces, Persian patterns and Chinese brushwork with it. Gallery 28 was designed as the 2009 redevelopment's thesis statement: its cases deliberately pair objects that could only exist because cultures had already met, traded and borrowed.

subchapters.title: Islamic Middle East — Gallery 31
subchapters.text: The Islamic galleries gather ceramics, metalwork and glass from a civilisation that, while Europe was in its early medieval centuries, led the world in mathematics, medicine and sheer gorgeousness of design. Look for lustreware — pottery with a metallic sheen achieved by painting with metal oxides and firing in a reducing kiln, a technique guarded like a trade secret — and for the geometry: interlacing patterns that could extend to infinity, art as mathematics, avoiding images while achieving abundance. Calligraphy carries the word as decoration, on tiles, bowls and mosque lamps. Notice how many techniques here — lustre, enamelled glass — later travelled west into European craft. The collection includes the celebrated group of Islamic ceramics formed by Sir Alan Barlow and the Reitlinger collection, giving the gallery unusual depth in medieval Persian wares.

subchapters.title: Mughal India and India from AD 600 — Galleries 32 and 33
subchapters.text: The Indian story continues into the Mughal centuries: miniature paintings of court life in jewel-like detail, jade and rock-crystal objects carved for emperors, and textiles that were India's great export to the world. Mughal miniatures reward a nose-close look — a durbar scene contains a hundred portraits, each face individual. Alongside, the galleries of later Indian art show temple sculpture and bronzes, including processional figures made to be carried, dressed and bathed, art as a living participant rather than a display piece. From here the route crosses to the floor's other pole: Japan, and the moment West finally meets East as equals and rivals. Mughal painting here includes works from the imperial ateliers of Akbar and Jahangir, whose painters signed tiny portraits in margins — individual artists emerging from an anonymous workshop tradition.

chapters.caption: Eastern Art — Chinese ceramics, Japanese prints, Islamic art and the samurai armour

chapters.title: West Meets East — Japan, Later China, and the Samurai
chapters.intro: Level 2 completes the Asian arc with later China and Japan, and the long, fascinated encounter between Asia and Europe: porcelain that bankrupted and inspired European factories, prints that changed Western painting, and armour made as much to be seen as to be fought in.

subchapters.title: Later China — Porcelain and Paintings
subchapters.text: China's later galleries hold what Europe dreamed about: porcelain. The Ashmolean's holdings of Chinese greenwares are described as the largest outside China, and the celadon cases — that sea-green glaze perfected a thousand years ago, pooled thick as glass in carved decoration — are the connoisseur's highlight. Then blue-and-white, the global bestseller, shipped by the million and copied from Delft to Isfahan. Look for pieces made expressly for export, with European shapes and coats of arms: Chinese workshops manufacturing to foreign order in the 1700s, globalisation in porcelain. The modern Chinese painting collection, among Europe's finest, closes the story in ink. The greenware collection's fame rests on the Hill collection of Chinese ceramics, long loaned and finally secured for the museum — celadons from Longquan kilns of the Song and Yuan dynasties.

subchapters.title: Japan — Prints, Lacquer, and Netsuke
subchapters.text: The Japanese galleries compress a civilisation into exquisite small scales. Look for woodblock prints — landscapes and actors whose flat colour and cropped compositions electrified European artists in the 1800s — and for netsuke, the miniature carved toggles that fastened pouches to kimono sashes: an entire bestiary and theatre company in boxwood and ivory, made to be held. Lacquerware, built up in dozens of layers, and ceramics for the tea ceremony, deliberately rustic, complete a display that teaches Japanese aesthetics by contrast: perfection and imperfection, each prized in its place. Everything here rewards the closest looking in the museum. The print collection includes works by Hokusai and Hiroshige; Oxford's holdings grew through 19th-century collectors who bought Japanese art when London dealers could hardly give it away.

subchapters.title: The Samurai Armour
subchapters.text: Now the object everyone photographs: a full suit of Japanese armour, all lacquered iron plates laced together with silk cord, beautiful and faintly menacing. Armour like this — a tosei-gusoku — was as much heraldry as protection: the colours of the silk lacing, the crest on the helmet and the dramatic mask announced whose retainer you were before a blow was struck. Look at the construction up close: hundreds of small scales, each lacquered against rust, articulated so the wearer could draw a bow or sword. It stands in the galleries as the martial pole of a culture whose other pole is the tea bowl — and the same patrons commissioned both. This armour dates to the Edo period, when Japan was at peace — it was made largely for ceremony and display, which explains the silk, the crest and the immaculate preservation.

subchapters.title: The Namikawa Cloisonne Vase
subchapters.text: Find the vase with a waterfall over rocks by Namikawa Yasuyuki, made around 1910 to 1915 — one of the museum's ten highlights and a summit of Japanese cloisonne enamel. Namikawa's Kyoto workshop produced enamel of jewel quality: wires finer than hair separating colours that shade like watercolour, on a black ground polished to mirror depth. Meiji-era Japan made such objects partly for export exhibitions, where they served as national ambassadors of skill, winning prizes in Paris and Chicago. Stand close and find the wire outlines in the mist. That this surface is metal and glass, not paint, is the whole miracle. Namikawa Yasuyuki's workshop employed dozens of craftsmen in Kyoto; his black-ground enamels won prizes at international exhibitions from Philadelphia to Paris, advertising Meiji Japan's mastery.

subchapters.title: When Europe Copied Asia
subchapters.text: Close the Asian floors with the traffic in the other direction: European ceramics straining to imitate Chinese porcelain before the secret of true porcelain was cracked at Meissen in 1708; Japanese prints re-composed by Van Gogh; Indian chintz so coveted that England banned its import to protect home weavers. The floor's title, West Meets East, is not a meeting of strangers but of old trading partners who had been copying each other for centuries. You have now crossed Asia. Next, we come home: England's treasures and the European art galleries, where the museum keeps a jewel made for a king who taught himself to read. The traffic produced hybrid masterpieces displayed across these floors — Delftware tulip vases in Chinese taste, Japanese lacquer mounted in French ormolu — objects with two homelands.

chapters.title: England's Treasures — The Alfred Jewel and Company
chapters.intro: Level 2's England galleries gather the museum's most storied British objects: a jewel inscribed by a king, a painting that helped invent perspective, and the drawings cabinet where Raphael and Michelangelo wait under low light. Small rooms, giant stories — budget your wonder accordingly.

subchapters.title: The Alfred Jewel
subchapters.text: Look for a teardrop of gold, enamel and rock crystal, small enough to hide in your fist: the Alfred Jewel, made in the late ninth century and inscribed around its edge, in Old English, 'AELFRED MEC HEHT GEWYRCAN' — Alfred ordered me to be made. Alfred the Great, king of Wessex, scholar-king who promoted translation and learning while fighting the Vikings, is the only plausible Alfred. The jewel is thought to be the head of an aestel, a reading pointer sent with his translations to his bishops. It was found at North Petherton in Somerset in 1693, near Alfred's refuge at Athelney. Under the crystal, an enamelled figure holds two plants — sight, or a saint, or Christ; scholars still argue, happily.

subchapters.title: Uccello's Hunt in the Forest
subchapters.text: Paolo Uccello's The Hunt in the Forest, painted around 1470, is the Renaissance's love affair with perspective staged as a night hunt: horsemen, hounds and deer converging into a dark wood along lines you can almost rule with a ruler, every spear and stag placed on the geometry. Uccello was, Vasari said, so obsessed with perspective he would stay up all night muttering about its sweetness. The picture is also simply gorgeous — gold on the harness, red coats against blue-green dark. It is one of the museum's ten highlights and the anchor of its early Renaissance paintings. Stand centred, at distance: the forest swallows the hunt, and you, along its vanishing point. The painting's original location is unknown — it may have decorated a Florentine palace chamber; its nocturnal gold-flecked surface suggests it was made to glitter by candlelight.

subchapters.title: Raphael and Michelangelo Drawings
subchapters.text: The Ashmolean's drawings collection is a national treasure shown in whispers: works on paper by Raphael, Michelangelo and Leonardo, kept in low light and rotated, so check what is out today. A Raphael drawing is as close as you can get to watching a Renaissance mind think — studies for altarpieces, heads turned three ways on one sheet, chalk moving faster than doubt. The museum's Raphael holdings are among the most important outside Italy, and its Michelangelo studies likewise. If the drawings gallery is showing them, stop everything and look, slowly. These sheets were never meant as public art; they are the workshop floor of genius, preserved. The drawings entered the museum through great bequests, including the Douce and Ruskin collections; John Ruskin himself gave drawings to Oxford for teaching, insisting students learn from originals.

subchapters.title: The Pissarro Archive and Sickert
subchapters.text: For a gentler room, find the Pissarro family archive — paintings, prints, drawings and letters of Camille Pissarro and his artist children and grandchildren, the largest such family archive in any museum, given by the family itself. Nearby, the Sickert room gathers Walter Sickert and his contemporaries: smoky Edwardian interiors and music-hall scenes, British modernism finding its feet. The contrast with Uccello, four centuries earlier in the same suite, is the European art floor's pleasure — a walkable argument about what painting is for, conducted by the paintings themselves. Take one picture per room home in your memory; more is greed. Lucien Pissarro settled in England and founded the Eragny Press; the archive's letters between father and son are a beloved source for historians of Impressionism's English chapter.

subchapters.title: The Messiah Stradivarius
subchapters.text: In the music displays, look for a violin of almost unnatural perfection: the 'Messiah' Stradivari, made by Antonio Stradivari in Cremona in 1716, in his golden period, and preserved in near-mint condition because it was barely ever played — passed between collectors like a relic rather than used as a tool. It came to the Ashmolean in 1939 and is never played now; its value is as evidence, the maker's varnish, tool marks and geometry intact for study. Musicians have mixed feelings — a silent Stradivarius is a paradox — but as a document of the greatest violin maker who ever lived, nothing on Earth is cleaner. The Messiah's near-perfect varnish made it controversial — some once doubted its authenticity precisely because it looked too new; dendrochronology and expert examination have confirmed the 1716 date.

chapters.caption: Western Art galleries — Turner, the Pre-Raphaelites, and the Alfred Jewel nearby

chapters.title: European Art 1800 to Today — Pre-Raphaelites, Turner, and the Rooftop
chapters.intro: Level 3M holds European art from 1800 onward: the Pre-Raphaelites in their Oxford heartland, Turner's watercolours, De Morgan ceramics and the moderns. Then we finish as the building intends — on the Level 4 rooftop, with coffee above the spires, and a strategy for everything you missed.

subchapters.title: The Pre-Raphaelites — Gallery 66
subchapters.text: Oxford was Pre-Raphaelite home turf, and Gallery 66 is their stronghold. In 1848 Rossetti, Millais and Holman Hunt founded the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, rebelling against academic convention in favour of intense colour, literary subjects and observed truth — painting medieval ladies and biblical scenes blade of grass by blade of grass. The Ashmolean's collection, fed by Oxford patrons like Thomas Combe of the University Press, is definitive: look for Holman Hunt's and Millais's jewel-bright canvases and the portraits of the circle's women, drawn and redrawn. Ruskin, their champion, taught drawing in this city. These pictures scandalised the Victorians and decorated a million student walls ever after. Thomas Combe, printer to the university, bought the young Brotherhood's works when few others would; his widow Martha bequeathed the collection that still anchors this gallery.

subchapters.title: Turner and the View of the High
subchapters.text: Look for J. M. W. Turner's watercolours and his famous view of Oxford's High Street — 'the finest street in England' painted by its greatest landscape artist, all golden stone and bustle beneath a luminous sky. Turner's Oxford connection ran deep: he painted the city repeatedly, and the Ashmolean holds a significant group of his watercolours, shown in rotation. Watercolour was Turner's laboratory — weather, light and dissolution tested on paper before the oil paintings made them famous. If the High is on display, compare it with the real street outside: same curve, same towers, two centuries of traffic apart. Few museum experiences close a loop that neatly. Turner's View of the High Street, Oxford, exhibited in 1810, was commissioned for a local print-seller — the artist was paid partly in the engravings that spread the image across Britain.

subchapters.title: Nineteenth-Century Art and De Morgan — Galleries 64 and 67
subchapters.text: The 19th-century galleries broaden the frame: French and British painting from Constable's naturalism to the Impressionists, with the Pissarro holdings giving this floor unusual depth in Camille's rural scenes. Then find William De Morgan's ceramics — lustred tiles and chargers painted with galleons, peacocks and fantastic beasts, their ruby and gold lustre reviving the Islamic techniques you saw two floors below. De Morgan, friend of William Morris, represents the Arts and Crafts conviction that beauty belonged in useful things. The galleries reward unhurried drifting; this is the floor where personal favourites ambush you from unexpected walls. De Morgan's lustre technique was a rediscovery — he spent years reverse-engineering Hispano-Moresque pottery, and his Fulham kilns' failures, he joked, taught him more than his successes.

subchapters.title: Modern Art — Gallery 62
subchapters.text: The modern rooms carry the story to the present: Picasso prints, British modernists, and the rotating contemporary displays under the Ashmolean NOW banner, which invite living artists to respond to the historic collections — a contemporary installation answering a classical gallery is the museum's founding idea, cultures crossing, still running. After half a million years, ending with art being made now is the honest finish. Note which single modern work you would take home; the exercise concentrates the mind wonderfully. Then take the lift to Level 4. You have earned the roof. The museum's contemporary programme began remarkably early — it was buying living artists in the 19th century — and the Ashmolean NOW series continues that founding habit of collecting the present.

subchapters.title: The Rooftop Terrace
subchapters.text: End on the roof. The Level 4 restaurant and terrace sit above Cockerell's facade, looking over the Randolph Hotel to the towers and domes of the colleges — the dreaming spires doing their thing while you drink coffee among them. It is a working restaurant, popular at lunch, but the terrace doubles as the museum's decompression chamber: the place to let Egypt, Crete, China and Raphael settle into one visit. From here, read the skyline you will explore on foot — St Mary's spire, the Radcliffe Camera's dome, Tom Tower at Christ Church. Oxford from above is a map of everything this museum has been telling you: learning, made visible in stone. The rooftop restaurant, opened with the 2009 building, was Oxford's first rooftop dining space — the view takes in the spires of St Mary's, All Souls and Christ Church in one sweep.
subchapters.directions: Ride the atrium lift to Level 4 for the rooftop restaurant and terrace.
subchapters.caption: The rooftop terrace — Oxford's spires from above the Ashmolean

subchapters.title: Wrap-Up — You Can't See It All (And That's Fine)
subchapters.text: A last word before Beaumont Street: you cannot see half a million years in one visit, and you shouldn't try. What you have done is the highlights spine — the museum's own story, money and writing, Egypt, the Aegean, Greece and Rome, the casts, Asia in both directions, the Alfred Jewel, and art to the present day. The natural sequel is the special exhibitions on Level 3, ticketed and changing, and a return for whichever gallery grabbed you hardest. Notice where you stand: the Bodleian and Radcliffe Square are minutes east, the History of Science Museum — in the original 1683 Ashmolean building — is across Broad Street. The first public museum in the world is still free, still working, still here tomorrow.
subchapters.directions: Exit onto Beaumont Street; Radcliffe Square and Broad Street are a few minutes' walk east.
subchapters.caption: Half a million years in one building — the Ashmolean at dusk

intro: The Ashmolean is the world's first public museum — opened in 1683, when the very idea that ordinary people could walk in and look at wonders was radical. Today it's Oxford University's museum of art and archaeology: half a million years of human creativity in one elegant building on Beaumont Street, and free. Our route climbs through time: the museum's own story, ancient Egypt and the classical world, the atmospheric Cast Gallery, Asia's Silk Road treasures, Western art from Raphael drawings to the Pre-Raphaelites, and the story of money itself — finishing on the rooftop terrace above Oxford's spires. Allow two hours, and don't try to see everything. Nobody can. That's the point.
mapNote: The Ashmolean stacks five levels behind its Beaumont Street façade. Lower Ground Floor: the Ashmolean Story, Money Gallery, Textiles, and Conservation. Ground Floor: the Ancient World — Egypt and Sudan, the Greek World, Rome, the Aegean, plus the Cast Gallery in the old building's east wing. Level 1: Asian Crossroads begins; Level 2: West Meets East (later Asian and Islamic art). Level 3: special exhibitions. Level 3M: European (Western) Art. Level 4: rooftop restaurant and terrace. Lifts and stairs sit in the modern central atrium — because the building weaves old and new wings, different parts of the same level aren't always connected, so use the atrium lifts to move between sections and check the floor plan.
practical: Admission to the permanent galleries is free; special exhibitions on Level 3 are ticketed. The museum is open daily, typically 10:00–17:00.
Pick up the free floor plan at the welcome desk — the building's mix of 1845 and 2009 wings is genuinely confusing without one, and it includes a '10 highlights in an hour' trail.
Don't try to see everything: half a million years of objects live here. Follow this guide's highlights route, then double back to whatever grabbed you.

The Cast Gallery and Western Art drawings are the connoisseur stops most visitors miss — if Raphael or Michelangelo drawings are on display, prioritise them; they're shown in rotation and not always out.
The rooftop restaurant is popular — book ahead for lunch, or just use the terrace for coffee and the view over Oxford.
Saturday coin-handling sessions in the Money Gallery let you hold real historic coins — free, drop-in, and great if you're visiting with kids.
Large bags may need to go in the lockers; travel light and keep your camera handy — photography (no flash) is allowed in most permanent galleries.
